title: Genesis 19:12–29
context: The angels warn Lot to take his household out of Sodom. His sons-in-law treat the warning as a joke. Lot lingers; they seize his hand—the LORD being merciful—and set him outside. He is granted flight to little Zoar. Sulfur and fire fall; Lot’s wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. Abraham looks toward the plain, and the narrator names why Lot lived: God remembered Abraham.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Mercy dragging Lot out, and fire on the cities of the plain: older Arminian and Reformed writers, each in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: It was not time to trifle, when the destruction was just at the door. But he seemed to them as one that mocked—They thought perhaps that the assault which the Sodomites had just now made upon his house had disturbed his head, and put him into such a fright that be knew not what he said. They that made a jest of every thing, made a jest of that, and so perished in the overthrow.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 19:14)

reformed.quote: At length the angels declare for what purpose they came, and what they were about to do. For so great was the indignity of the last act of this people, that Lot must now see how impossible it was for God to bear with them any longer. And, in the first place, they declare, that they are come to destroy the city, because the cry of it was waxen great.

verses.text: The men said to Lot, “Do you have anybody else here? Sons-in-law, your sons, your daughters, and whomever you have in the city, bring them out of the place:
verses.arminianNotes:
The visitors ask who else is Lot’s—sons-in-law, your sons, your daughters, anyone in the city—and tell him to bring them out. Warning is spoken so a household may actually flee.

One hears mercy offered, not a closed list. Grace enables flight; Lot is responsible to gather those he can. The door of escape is sincerely opened to all he will bring.
verses.reformedNotes:
Anyone Lot has in the city is named for rescue while the sentence on the place is already moving. The question is whom mercy will pull out.

Reformed readers hear particular deliverance. God is gathering a remnant, not reopening Sodom’s case. Judgment proceeds; rescue is for those He will bring out.

verses.text: for we will destroy this place, because the outcry against them has grown so great before the LORD that the LORD has sent us to destroy it.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Destruction is near because the outcry against the people has grown so great before the LORD, who has sent these messengers to destroy. Heaven has heard wickedness, not a rumor.

The warning is timed and moral. God judges after outcry. Those who hear still have a moment to take the offered flight.
verses.reformedNotes:
The outcry has become great, that the LORD has sent them to destroy. Judicial judgment is commissioned, not guessed at.

God is Judge of cities as of persons. What Genesis 18 heard, Genesis 19 now carries out. Wrath here is holy, not impulsive.

verses.text: Lot went out, and spoke to his sons-in-law, who were pledged to marry his daughters, and said, “Get up! Get out of this place, for the LORD will destroy the city!” But he seemed to his sons-in-law to be joking.
verses.arminianNotes:
Lot goes out and urges his sons-in-law: Get out—the LORD is going to destroy the city. They take him for a jester. A true warning can still be mocked.

Classical Arminians grieve this as responsible unbelief. Grace enabled Lot to speak; they were not forced to scoff. Mercy offered can be refused; jesting at judgment is their choice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Lot warns; the sons-in-law hear a joke. Unbelief can sit inside a household that has been told the truth.

Treating the LORD’s sentence as jest does not delay it. Lot’s word is not emptied by their laugh; the destroyers still come.

verses.text: When the morning came, then the angels hurried Lot, saying, “Get up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be consumed in the iniquity of the city.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Dawn comes, and the angels urge again: take your wife and your two daughters who are here, or you will be consumed. The summons is repeated and aimed at those still within reach.

Assisting grace keeps calling. “Up!” is a command they can obey this morning. Responsible flight is how sweeping-away is refused.
verses.reformedNotes:
Morning does not soften the sentence. The angels urge because punishment will sweep the city, and those “who are here” are the remnant still to be led out.

Urgency is mercy inside a fixed judgment. The command is the means of the deliverance God is already putting into motion.

verses.text: But he lingered; and the men grabbed his hand, his wife’s hand, and his two daughters’ hands, the LORD being merciful to him; and they took him out, and set him outside of the city.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But he lingered.” Even warned, Lot delays. Then they seize him, his wife, and both daughters by the hand—the LORD was merciful to him—and set them outside. Mercy that takes the hand is still mercy.

Arminians do not deny the grip. Lingered hearts need more than advice. Yet lingering was Lot’s hesitation, and the way out remains a grace-enabled going he must continue.
verses.reformedNotes:
He lingered, so they seized him. The narrator names the cause: the LORD being merciful. Deliverance here is effectual—hands on theirs, feet set outside the city.

God does not wait for Lot’s pace to become heroic. Mercy that saves can overrule delay without calling delay faith. The remnant is outside because God took hold.

verses.text: It came to pass, when they had taken them out, that he said, “Escape for your life! Don’t look behind you, and don’t stay anywhere in the plain. Escape to the mountains, lest you be consumed!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Escape for your life! Don’t look back or stop in the plain. Escape to the mountains, lest you be swept away. The path is plain: flee, and do not linger in sight of what God is judging.

In practice: grace has set them outside; they must now run. Looking back is a resistible pull. The warning treats them as agents who can still obey.
verses.reformedNotes:
Life depends on flight, and flight has a path: not the valley, not a backward glance, but the hills. The same mercy that seized now commands.

Lest you be swept away is not theater. God appoints both the rescue and the manner of it. Safety is in His word, not in Lot’s sense of the map.

verses.text: Lot said to them, “Oh, not so, my lord.
verses.arminianNotes:
Lot answers, “Oh, not so, my lord. See now.” Freshly pulled out, he still bargains. Fear speaks; he does not simply run as told.

The note struck is a mixed heart. Mercy has been shown; now he must receive the next instruction. “Oh, not so” is Lot’s own word, not a script he could not refuse.
verses.reformedNotes:
The man set outside still objects. Deliverance has not made him bold. God will hear the plea without surrendering the judgment.

Remaining fear does not unmake the mercy already taken. The LORD’s purpose to save Lot can bear a trembling mouth and still keep the remnant.

verses.text: See now, your servant has found favor in your sight, and you have magnified your loving kindness, which you have shown to me in saving my life. I can’t escape to the mountain, lest evil overtake me, and I die.
verses.arminianNotes:
Lot confesses favor, kindness, and a saved life—then says he can’t escape to the mountain, lest disaster overtake him. Gratitude and unbelief share a sentence.

He names mercy truly, then shrinks from the commanded path. Grace-enabled flight still asks for trust. Fear is understandable; it is not the same as wisdom.
verses.reformedNotes:
He admits great kindness in saving his life, then pleads inability. The remnant’s weakness is on the page.

God has already saved; Lot’s “I can’t” does not veto that mercy. Providence can grant a nearer city without making fear the author of rescue.

verses.text: See now, this city is near to flee to, and it is a little one. Oh let me escape there (isn’t it a little one?), and my soul will live.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He points to a nearby “little” city: let me escape there, and my life will be saved. Zoar is requested as a smaller, nearer refuge than the hills.

Classical Arminians see petition, not seizure. Lot asks. Mercy offered may stoop to a weaker faith, and he remains responsible to go where he is then sent.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Isn’t it a little one?” is bargaining geography. God can spare a town as a corridor for the remnant.

Even the requested city sits inside the LORD’s government. Lot’s life will be saved because mercy governs the map, not because smallness is a loophole.

verses.text: He said to him, “Behold, I have granted your request concerning this thing also, that I will not overthrow the city of which you have spoken.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I have granted your request concerning this thing also”—the city will not be overthrown. Added kindness meets the plea. God is not stingy with the man He has begun to save.

Further favor is sincerely given. Lot asked; heaven granted. Mercy can include a nearer shelter without cancelling the call to escape quickly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Favor is granted, not earned: this city will stand. The Judge who rains fire can also withhold it from one town.

Additional mercy is as sovereign as the first. God determines what He will not overthrow for the remnant’s sake, and He says so.

verses.text: Hurry, escape there, for I can’t do anything until you get there.” Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar.
verses.arminianNotes:
Escape there quickly; “I can’t do anything until you get.” Zoar means little. Judgment waits on Lot’s arrival—an astonishing kindness that still requires haste.

Delay is no longer safe. Grace has opened Zoar; responsible obedience is to run there now. Mercy is not permission to linger at the rim of the valley.
verses.reformedNotes:
The destroyer waits until Lot arrives. Effectual deliverance even times the fire. Zoar is named for its smallness, and it stands because God said it would.

“I can’t do anything until you get” is appointed patience, not weakness. The remnant must be in place before judicial judgment falls.

verses.text: The sun had risen on the earth when Lot came to Zoar.
verses.arminianNotes:
Sunrise, and Lot comes to Zoar. The hour of arrival is dated by the sun. He did, at last, enter the little city granted him.

Classical Arminians honor the arriving. Grace enabled the flight; Lot actually came. Morning light meets a man who took the opened way—late, lingering, and still saved by going where he was sent.
verses.reformedNotes:
The sun is up when Lot reaches Zoar. Providence clocks the remnant into shelter as day begins.

Arrival is God’s timing as much as Lot’s steps. The little city of refuge is occupied because mercy meant him there when fire fell.

verses.text: Then the LORD rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the LORD out of the sky.
verses.arminianNotes:
Then the LORD rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the LORD out of the. Brimstone is the LORD’s own rain on cities whose outcry had become great.

God judges after warning and outcry. The very Lord who offered flight now acts. This is holy sorrow, not a cue for later contempt of persons.
verses.reformedNotes:
Sulfur and fire fall “from the LORD out of the.” Judicial judgment is the LORD’s work, twice named.

Heaven is not a bystander. What Genesis 18 announced, Genesis 19 performs. God rains what He has decreed; the remnant is already in Zoar.

verses.text: He overthrew those cities, all the plain, all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew on the ground.
verses.arminianNotes:
He overthrew those cities, the valley, the inhabitants, and that which grew on the ground. The judgment is total for that place—people and pasture together.

Arminian interpreters do not minimize this. Wickedness has an end. Mercy had been offered in flight; overthrow is what refusal meets. The text is grief, not a license to hate.
verses.reformedNotes:
Cities, valley, inhabitants, vegetation: the overthrow is comprehensive. The Judge of all the earth does what is just.

Nothing here is accidental blight. The remnant’s escape makes the sentence clearer, not crueler. Judicial judgment is holy.

verses.text: But Lot’s wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.
verses.arminianNotes:
Lot’s wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt. “Don’t look behind you, and don’t stay” was an earnest command; she treated it as optional. Divided love can stand a few yards from rescue and still turn.

Remember Lot’s wife. Grace had seized her hand; she remained responsible not to gaze at what God was judging. Looking back is a live, resistible act.
verses.reformedNotes:
Behind him, she looked back, and salt is the memorial. The command of verse 17 is now a grave.

Proximity to Lot is not salvation. God meant the warning; her glance meets judicial judgment even on the road of flight. Mercy that seizes still requires the path He named.

verses.text: Abraham went up early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
Abraham goes early to the place where he had stood before the LORD—the intercession ground of chapter 18. He returns to prayer’s geography to see what the Judge has done.

Classical Arminians honor this watching. The friend of God does not gloat; he goes to the standing-place of plea. Intercession was sincere; now he will look at the answer.
verses.reformedNotes:
Early morning, Abraham stands again where he stood before the LORD. The intercessor is taken back to the scene of the dialogue.

The place of prayer is also the place of providence. God who heard Abraham will now show him the valley.

verses.text: He looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward all the land of the plain, and saw that the smoke of the land went up as the smoke of a furnace.
verses.arminianNotes:
He looks toward Sodom and Gomorrah and the land of the plain: smoke going up as the smoke of a furnace. What he sees is judgment completed, not a rumor.

The furnace-smoke is the end of a people who would not repent. Abraham’s looking is witness, not triumph. Mercy had been sought for the city; ten righteous were not found.
verses.reformedNotes:
Behold: smoke like a furnace. The well-watered valley is now a column of burning.

Abraham sees what God has done. Judicial judgment is public enough for the patriarch to read it on the skyline. The LORD keeps His word to judge—and, as the next verse says, to remember.

verses.text: When God destroyed the cities of the plain, God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the middle of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in which Lot lived.
verses.arminianNotes:
When God destroyed the cities of the plain, God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the middle of the overthrow. Lot lives because mercy ran through Abraham’s standing before the LORD.

Arminian readers hear remembrance as covenant kindness that still treats Lot as a man sent out. Intercession was not ignored. Grace remembered, and Lot was actually brought out.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator’s verdict: God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out. Effectual deliverance is anchored in God’s covenant regard for the patriarch.

Lot’s rescue is not luck, nor merely Lot’s last-minute run. The God who judged the valley remembered His friend and pulled the nephew from the midst. Remnant mercy rides on God’s faithfulness.
